Shows prayer performed and emptied of meaning, the same gap between an act and a state.
Describes charity cancelled by display, which is this ayah's reasoning applied to giving.

studies.applyIt: Pick one thing you do that is visibly religious, a prayer or a donation or a fast, and ask what you would still do about it if nobody ever found out. Change nothing yet. The ayah is interested in what actually crosses over from an act, and that question is the only instrument you have for finding out.

studies.title: Permission Given To The Wronged
studies.meaning: Two short statements, then a shift. God defends those who believe, and God has no love for the persistent betrayer. Then permission is granted, and the ground given for it is a single fact: they were wronged. The passive voice is doing work here, since the people addressed are described as being fought rather than as fighting. The final clause adds that God is able to give them victory, which separates the permission from any promise about how it will turn out.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, and the classical commentators broadly report this as the first passage permitting the community to fight, after years in Mecca in which they had been told to hold back. The believers had been driven from their homes and had reached Medina under pressure. The wording is unusually careful about grounds: it does not authorise a cause, it responds to a wrong already established.

keyTerms.note: A verb form suggesting repeated warding rather than one act. The intensive pattern makes the defending continuous, which is why the sentence needs no object naming the threat.
An intensive form of the word for someone who breaks a trust. The pattern names a habit rather than an incident, so the statement concerns character and not a single betrayal.
A passive with no named giver, which is how the Quran often marks a divine act. Its passivity matters here: the permission arrives from outside, it is not claimed.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Vengeance in that world required no permission. A tribe raided, another raided back, and the cycle was governed by custom rather than by any grant of leave from anyone. What is strange about this passage in its own setting is that it treats fighting as something needing authorisation at all, and that it identifies who may by what was done to them rather than by who they are.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for permission is a passive verb with no stated subject, and it stands as the first word of the ayah. Arabic word order gives that position weight, so the sentence opens on the grant itself rather than on the people receiving it. The reason follows only afterwards, in a short clause naming the wrong done to them.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage rests the justification for fighting entirely on a prior wrong, and it locates the grant outside the community that benefits from it. Both moves limit rather than release. It also places God's defence of the believers in the sentence before the permission, so that human action is framed as happening inside a protection already given, and not as substituting for one that is missing.

crossReferences.why: Sets a limit in the same terms, against those who fight, with transgression ruled out.
Names the oppressed praying for a protector as the reason the question arises at all.
Weighs driving people from the Sacred Mosque as heavier than the fighting itself.

studies.applyIt: Think about the last time you were wronged and did nothing, and the last time you answered back within a minute. The difference between those two is usually energy rather than principle. This passage grants a response and grounds it wholly in the wrong that came first. Try naming, for one grievance you still carry, exactly what was done. No more than that.

studies.title: Places Where God Is Remembered
studies.meaning: The people just given permission are identified twice over: by what was done to them, and by what they said. They were driven from their homes for saying that God is their Lord. Then the ayah widens far past that community. Were God not checking people by means of one another, four kinds of building would have been pulled down, and they are named in order, monasteries, churches, synagogues, mosques. Other communities come first, and all four are described by the same activity.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, immediately after the permission to fight. The believers had left property and standing behind in Mecca. Commentators read the list of buildings as the reason the permission is given rather than as an aside: restraint placed on aggression is presented as what keeps worship of any kind standing anywhere. No specific occasion is reported beyond the emigration itself.

keyTerms.note: A noun from the verb to push back. It describes restraint applied to people through other people, so the balance in view is held by resistance rather than by an absence of conflict.
A word for the towers or cells of solitary devotees. It occurs only here in the Quran, and it names the most withdrawn form of worship at the very head of the list.
From a root meaning inaccessible and strong at once. Paired with strength at the close, it grounds the whole argument in what God is rather than in what people manage to achieve.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabia's edges held Christian monasteries, and travellers used them as landmarks and as shelter. Jewish communities in Yathrib and the northern oases kept their own houses of study and prayer. None of this was abstract to the first listeners. These were buildings on roads people had ridden, kept by people they had bought grain from, and their destruction was something armies in the region did as a matter of routine.
studies.didYouKnow: This is the only ayah in the Quran that mentions monasteries, and the word it uses for them occurs nowhere else in the text. It is also the only place where four kinds of house of worship are listed together. The order runs from the most secluded form of worship outward, and the mosque is named last rather than first.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah gives a reason for permitting force, and the reason is the survival of worship in general rather than the survival of one community. That is a significant widening: the buildings of other faiths fall under the same protection and are named ahead of the community's own. It also identifies the only offence of the expelled as a sentence they spoke, making the wrong done to them a matter of speech and belief.

crossReferences.why: States the same principle of checking people by one another, there inside the account of David.
Sets out relations with those who neither fought over religion nor drove anyone from home.
Rules out compulsion in religion, which is the principle these protected buildings rest upon.

studies.applyIt: Find out this week where the nearest place of worship that is not yours actually stands: the church, the synagogue, the temple down the road. You do not have to go inside. This ayah lists other people's buildings ahead of its own and gives them all the same description, and simply knowing where they are is a small way of taking that seriously.

studies.title: When We Give Them Power
studies.meaning: The sentence completes the one before it. God's help goes to those who support Him, and here is what such people look like once they hold the land. Four things follow, two turned inward and two turned outward: prayer kept standing, the charity given, right commanded, wrong refused. The test is placed after power rather than before it, which is the harder position. Then the last clause removes the final claim they might make, since the outcome of all matters belongs to God.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, closing the passage that permitted the community to defend itself. They had just been given a right, and the ayah immediately describes what they would do with an authority they did not yet hold. Commentators note the order: conduct under power is described after the permission rather than before it, and it is applied to a community rather than to a ruler.

keyTerms.note: A verb for giving someone a secure footing and the means to act. It covers land, authority and capacity at once, so the condition described is any real power to shape things.
From the verb to know. It names good that a society already recognises rather than a code imposed on it, which is what makes commanding it possible in the first place.
From the root for what follows behind. It names the last stage of a matter rather than its result in the moment, and the ayah assigns that stage to God alone.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Power in Arabia was tribal and unstable. A clan that won a season of dominance took the wells, the grazing and the right to levy on caravans, and there was no assumption that it owed anything to anyone outside itself. Ascendancy was expected to be spent on the clan. A description of what a group would do once on top, phrased in duties rather than in spoils, described a different arrangement entirely.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase for the outcome of all matters occurs only twice in the Quran, here and in the thirty-first surah. The verb for being established in the land appears in this exact form in one other place, where it describes generations given an even firmer footing and then destroyed. The two uses read as each other's answer.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah answers a question religion often leaves open: what a movement becomes when it stops being persecuted. It defines that stage by four practices rather than by an outcome, and it hands the outcome to God in the final clause, which takes success off the list of things being promised. Power is treated as a condition to be described, never as an achievement to be enjoyed.

crossReferences.why: Promises succession in the land to the believers and describes the worship expected to follow it.
Uses the same pairing of commanding right and refusing wrong to define a whole community.
Carries the only other occurrence of the phrase about the outcome of all matters.

studies.applyIt: Think of a place where you hold more say than the people around you: a team, a household, a group you help run. Ask what you have actually done with that in the last month. This ayah describes people at the moment power arrives, and it lists what they keep doing rather than what they finally get to do.

studies.title: They Denied Before Them
studies.meaning: Consolation arrives as a list. If they call you a liar, the passage says, then start counting: the people of Noah, then two vanished Arabian peoples, then the people of Abraham and of Lot. The names come without any of their stories attached, which is the point, since the audience is assumed to know them. What the sequence establishes is that rejection is the ordinary reception of a messenger, and not a sign that something has gone wrong with this one.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, though the passage speaks to a pressure that had built through the Meccan years. Commentators place these ayat at the surah's turn from the pilgrimage toward the community's opponents. The peoples named were familiar from ruins and trade routes rather than from books, and the passage assumes its listeners can supply the rest of each account from memory.

keyTerms.note: A verb stronger than disbelieving. It accuses the speaker of deliberate falsehood, which is why the consolation that follows concerns the person and not only the message he carries.
The word ties a community to its men and its lineage. Repeating it for each rejection makes the pattern collective, so what is described is a society's refusal rather than an individual's.
A people remembered in Arabia long before the Quran, known from ruins in the northern Hijaz. Naming them beside Noah sets local memory and older sacred history in one list without marking the seam.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Trade routes north ran past ruins everyone could see. Rock-cut facades in the northern Hijaz were pointed out to travellers as the work of a vanished people, and caravan guides told their stories at the halts. When these ayat name such peoples with no explanation, they draw on something closer to landscape than to scripture. The audience had ridden past the evidence themselves.
studies.didYouKnow: These two ayat name five peoples across two short lines, with no story attached to any of them. Thamud is among the few peoples named in the Quran who also turn up in ancient records outside the Arabian tradition, in inscriptions and in classical geography, which is unusual for a name the text expects its listeners to recognise unaided.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Placing a living rejection inside a list of old ones changes what that rejection means. It stops being evidence against the message and becomes evidence that the message belongs to a known category. The passage also draws no line between peoples remembered locally and those from older sacred history, which treats prophecy as one continuous process rather than as a series of separate religions.

crossReferences.why: Tells of messengers before who were denied and endured patiently until help reached them.
Repeats the same consolation almost word for word, adding the scriptures those messengers carried.
States that nothing is said to this messenger which was not said to those before him.

studies.applyIt: The next time something you said is dismissed out of hand, resist the first instinct, which is to ask what was wrong with the way you said it. Sometimes nothing was. This passage answers a moment of rejection by handing over a list of older ones, and reading a list like that puts a bad afternoon back into proportion.

studies.theme: Time and the Brevity of Life
studies.title: Stilled Wells And Empty Palaces
studies.meaning: The list of rejected messengers closes with Moses, and then the register changes. A reprieve is described as something deliberately given, followed by a seizure, and a question is left hanging about what that rejection was like. The second ayah answers with a landscape rather than an argument: towns fallen in on their own roofs, a well nobody draws from, a high building standing empty. The ruins are the evidence, and no moral is attached to them.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in the surah's turn toward those denying the message. Classical commentators read the reprieve as the central point here: the delay before a reckoning is presented as a deliberate act rather than as the absence of one. No occasion of revelation is reported, and the towns are left unnamed, so the description covers far more than any single site.

keyTerms.note: From a root for extension and length of time. It pictures slack deliberately given rather than attention lapsing, so the delay in the passage is something done and not something missing.
A word for emptiness that has fallen in on itself. Paired here with roofs, it sinks the building onto its own supports rather than having it knocked down from outside.
Used of a well that still holds water but has nobody left to draw it. The word occurs once in the Quran, and it is the quietest image in the whole sentence.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A well was the reason a settlement existed at all. Digging one took months, maintaining it took a community, and its ownership was held in tribal memory across generations. A well standing unused meant not drought but the absence of people, which was a more disturbing sight than a ruined wall. Travellers on the northern routes passed exactly this: good water, cut stone, and nobody at all.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for the abandoned well occurs only once in the Quran. The word for the high building occurs twice, and the other passage uses it of towers built so well that death reaches people inside them anyway. The question closing the previous ayah, asking how God's rejection was, appears in this exact form five times across the text.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage separates delay from indifference, which is the specific anxiety it answers. A reprieve is described in the first person as something given, so the interval before consequence becomes part of the account rather than a gap in it. The ruins then supply proof without commentary. What is established is that time is not evidence, and a long silence carries no verdict either way.

crossReferences.why: States that respite given to wrongdoers is not for their good, which this passage assumes.
Points at houses standing empty through their people's wrongdoing, as a sign for those who know.
Sends the listener out to travel and look at how those before them ended.

studies.applyIt: If you pass an empty building on your way somewhere this week, stop for ten seconds and work out who used to be inside it. This passage answers a question about God's dealing with people by pointing at a landscape rather than by arguing. That habit, of reading a place for the people it lost, is what the ayah is training.

studies.title: The Blindness Of Hearts
studies.meaning: A question that turns into a definition. The ayah asks whether they have not travelled the land so as to have hearts that reason and ears that hear, which places understanding in two organs and makes travel the occasion for it. Then the famous correction: it is not the eyes that go blind, but the hearts inside the chests. The commentators note the added clause about the chests, which forecloses reading the heart as a metaphor for the mind alone.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The ayah follows a list of destroyed communities, ending with an image of ruined towns, stilled wells and abandoned mansions. Trade routes out of Arabia ran past several such sites, so the invitation to travel and look was not hypothetical. No specific occasion is reported. The passage is addressed to people who had walked past the evidence for years without it registering.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to tie or tether, as a camel is tethered. Reason in Arabic is the faculty that binds things together and holds a person back, which is why the Quran locates it in the heart.
The ordinary verb for losing sight, applied to an organ that does not see. Using the physical word rather than a metaphor for ignorance is what gives the sentence its force.

The clause naming where the hearts are is grammatically unnecessary, since hearts are not anywhere else. Commentators read the redundancy as emphasis, insisting the blindness is located in a person rather than in an idea.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Ruins were part of the landscape. The road north to Syria passed rock-cut tombs and abandoned settlements whose stories the caravans told and retold, and the road south passed dams and terraces that had failed. Merchants covered thousands of miles in a lifetime. The ayah is addressed to a travelling people and asks what all that distance actually produced, which is a pointed question to put to a merchant.
studies.didYouKnow: The ayah pairs hearts with reasoning and ears with hearing, and leaves the eyes out of the first half entirely. When they arrive in the second half it is only to be dismissed. The structure sets up the correction before it is made. This is one of the clearest places where the Quran treats the heart as an organ of perception rather than of feeling.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah relocates a failure that people usually place elsewhere. Not seeing is treated as a condition of the person rather than a shortage of evidence, which means more evidence would not solve it. That is a hard claim and it is also a hopeful one, since a condition can change while a shortage of proof cannot be argued out of. And by naming the heart as what reasons, the passage refuses the split between thinking and caring that most accounts of belief assume.

crossReferences.why: Describes hearts that do not understand, eyes that do not see, ears that do not hear.
Names a seal on hearts and hearing, and a covering over the sight.
Asks whether they reflect on the Quran, or whether there are locks on hearts.

studies.applyIt: Go somewhere old this month, and stand in it for ten minutes without taking a photograph. A graveyard, a ruin, a building older than your grandparents. The ayah connects travelling with understanding and then says the connection often fails. Ten minutes without documenting anything is the smallest test of whether it is failing for you.

studies.title: A Day Like A Thousand Years
studies.meaning: The demand behind the ayah is a taunt: bring on the punishment you keep describing. Two answers follow, and neither is a threat. First, God does not fail a promise, which moves the issue from whether to when. Then a measurement, deliberately unsettling: one day with your Lord is like a thousand years of the counting you do. The ayah does not say the reckoning is far off. It says the unit being used to measure it does not apply.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, addressing opponents who treated the delay of consequence as proof that none was coming. The commentators read the thousand years as a comparison rather than a conversion, illustrating the gap between two scales. They note that the Quran gives a different figure elsewhere, which supports reading these numbers as scale rather than as arithmetic.

keyTerms.gloss: they press you to hurry it
keyTerms.note: A verb form meaning to demand haste from someone. The pressure falls on the messenger rather than on God, which is what turns the demand into a taunt rather than a question.
From a root for coming behind or taking another's place. Applied to a promise it means failing to arrive at the appointed point, so the denial concerns timing as much as truth.
A verb of counting, addressed directly to the listeners. It marks the thousand years as belonging to human arithmetic, which is exactly the frame the sentence sets aside.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Time in Arabia was counted in what could be watched: moons, the season of rain, the arrival of a caravan, a debt falling due at the next pilgrimage. Nobody kept an abstract calendar of centuries. A thousand years was not a figure anyone used practically. It was the largest number that meant simply longer than memory, so naming it pointed past the edge of what could be counted at all.
studies.didYouKnow: This exact phrase about a day like a thousand years occurs once in the Quran. A related statement in the thirty-second surah gives a day whose measure is a thousand years of your counting, and a third passage names fifty thousand. The classical commentators treat the differing figures as descriptions of different things rather than as a discrepancy.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah declines to defend God's timetable and disqualifies the instrument being used to judge it instead. That is a different move from asking for patience. It grants the objection its facts, that nothing has happened yet, and denies that those facts mean what the objector thinks. What it establishes is that duration is a created thing, felt from inside, and not a measure that reaches God.

crossReferences.why: Gives a day whose measure is a thousand years, inside an account of affairs ascending to God.
Names a day of fifty thousand years, which is why these figures read as scale.
Answers the same demand for haste and notes that a term has already been appointed.

studies.applyIt: Notice the next time you check something too soon: a reply, a result, a change you were hoping to see in yourself. Count how many hours have actually passed. The taunt in this ayah and the ordinary impatience in that habit run on the same assumption, that the right interval is whichever one you can feel.

studies.title: Only A Plain Warner
studies.meaning: Four short ayat move from history to a job description to two outcomes. Towns were given rope while doing wrong, then seized, and the destination is God's. The messenger is then told to say what he is, and the sentence is unusually narrow: a plain warner, nothing more. What follows is the pair of outcomes he warns about, and the order carries weight. Forgiveness and generous provision come first; those who worked to defeat the message come second.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The surah has been arguing with people who demanded that the threatened punishment arrive at once, and here it draws that argument to a close. Commentators note the deliberate narrowing of the messenger's role in the middle ayah. He is not the one who brings a reckoning, only the one who states it, which answers the demand being made of him directly.

keyTerms.note: An active participle meaning both evident and clarifying. Attached to a warner it says the warning is unambiguous, which closes off the excuse that the message came in an unreadable form.
The word carries value and open-handedness at once. Applied to provision it describes both what is given and the manner of giving, which is why plain abundance does not translate it.
A participle for trying to render someone powerless or slip beyond their reach. It describes deliberate work against the message rather than simple disbelief, which is a narrower charge.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A herald in that world was a recognised figure. He carried terms between camps before a battle, announced a truce or a market, and his person was protected precisely because he decided nothing himself. Everyone understood that shouting at the herald changed no terms. A messenger describing himself as only a warner was using a role the audience already knew, with all the limits that came attached to it.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase describing a plain warner occurs in eleven places across the Quran, spoken by several different prophets, and here it stands as the entire content of what is to be said. The word for those working to thwart the revelation occurs three times in the text, and the other two sit together in a single later surah.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Narrowing the messenger's role protects both sides of the relationship. It denies him the power his opponents were daring him to use, and it keeps the reckoning entirely with God, where the passage has already placed the destination. The order of the two outcomes then does its own work: forgiveness is named before punishment, and it is paired with provision rather than with mere escape.

crossReferences.why: Divides the roles exactly, leaving delivery to the messenger and the reckoning with God.
Limits the messenger to reminding and states plainly that he is not set over people.
Describes messengers sent only as bearers of good news and as warners, nothing further.

studies.applyIt: Think of something you have been trying to make someone believe: a diagnosis, a risk, a change they need. Ask whether your part was ever more than saying it clearly, once. Most of the exhaustion in those conversations comes from taking on a role that was never yours. Say it plainly this week, and then stop.

studies.title: What God Makes Firm
studies.meaning: The ayah states a general condition of prophecy: no messenger or prophet was sent before without something being cast into his longing. Two verbs then answer it in sequence. God cancels what was cast, and God makes His signs firm. Commentators differ sharply over what the casting refers to and over the reports attached to this ayah, many treating those reports as unsound. What the sentence itself establishes is interference followed by correction, with the correction always God's.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan by placement, in a surah that joins material of both settings. Classical exegesis discusses reports of a specific occasion here, and records wide disagreement about them, with many scholars judging the reports weak and reading the ayah as a general statement about prophecy instead. The common ground across the commentators is that the ayah's subject is God's protection of revelation.

keyTerms.note: The verb covers wishing and also reciting aloud. That double sense is the reason classical readings of the ayah diverge, and the commentators record both possibilities without settling the matter.
From a root meaning both to copy and to erase. Here the erasing sense governs, and its object is what was cast in, never anything belonging to the revelation itself.
From the root behind wisdom and judgement. The verb pictures fixing something so it cannot be shifted, and it is given as the settled outcome rather than as one possible result.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Poets in Arabia were widely thought to receive their lines from an unseen companion, and a soothsayer's rhymed pronouncements were understood to arrive from outside him. That was the available model for inspired speech, and it was the accusation thrown most often at the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him). A passage separating what is cast in from what is confirmed speaks straight into that assumption.
studies.didYouKnow: This is the only place in the Quran where the words for messenger and for prophet stand side by side inside a single negative construction. The pairing widens the statement so that it covers every figure sent, leaving no category outside it. The two verbs that answer the interference, cancelling and then making firm, follow each other with nothing in between.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah grants that a prophet is a human being open to interference, then locates the guarantee of revelation entirely outside him. That is a strong claim about where reliability sits: not in the messenger's immunity but in God's correction. It also treats the interference as a general feature of prophecy rather than an exception, so a reader's confidence rests on a repeated act of God and not on one unblemished career.

crossReferences.why: States that God sent down the reminder and is its guardian, which is this ayah's conclusion.
Describes pressure applied to turn the Prophet aside, and the steadying that answered it.
Says falsehood cannot approach the revelation from before it or from behind it.

studies.applyIt: Take one belief you hold that you have never checked, and find out this week where you first got it. Not in order to discard it. The ayah describes something slipping in unnoticed and then being cleared away, and the clearing depends on somebody looking. Most of what we are sure of arrived without a receipt.

studies.title: Diseased Hearts And Hardened Ones
studies.meaning: A purpose clause explains what the interference described just before is permitted to do. It becomes a trial, and the ayah names exactly who it tests: those with a sickness in the heart, and those whose hearts have gone hard. Two different failures are being distinguished. One is an active corruption, the other a loss of feeling. The closing line places the wrongdoers in a split described as far off, meaning a division that has already travelled past repair.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, continuing directly from the ayah about revelation being confirmed. The community in Medina included people whose commitment was uncertain, and the phrase about sickness in the heart is used elsewhere in the Quran for exactly that group. Commentators read this ayah as explaining why a testing element is permitted at all, rather than as opening a new subject.

keyTerms.note: The root describes smelting metal to separate it from its ore. A trial in this sense reveals what was already present rather than adding anything, which is why it can be given as a purpose.
The Quran uses this word of hearts repeatedly, always for a condition that is hidden and progressive. It implies something once sound, which distinguishes it from the hardness named beside it.
From a root meaning to cleave in two, leaving each party on its own side. Called far off here, it describes a distance that has opened rather than a disagreement still being held.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Medina was a town of alliances rather than one tribe, and the community forming inside it held people bound by treaty, by marriage, or by calculation as much as by conviction. Loyalties were readable in small things: who attended, who lent money, who left early. Anything ambiguous entering that setting sorted people quickly, because everyone was already watching everyone else for the direction they would jump.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase describing a deep or far-reaching split occurs three times in the Quran. One of the others concerns people disputing over a revealed book, and the third concerns turning away after the message has become clear, so all three attach this same phrase to division over revelation rather than to ordinary conflict.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah gives a purpose to something unsettling, which is a hard thing to state honestly. It does not say the interference is good; it says what the interference separates. That places the value in the sorting rather than in the trial. It also splits the failure into two kinds, sickness and hardness, which resists a single explanation for why people turn away and leaves room for two different histories.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same phrase for a sickness in the heart which God increases as it runs its course.
Describes hearts made hard after a covenant, the second of the two conditions named here.
Speaks of the bad being sorted from the good and heaped together, the same image of separation.

studies.applyIt: There is usually one thing you know you avoid thinking about, because thinking about it would require a change. Name it once today, in a single sentence, without deciding anything. This ayah distinguishes a heart that has gone hard from one that is unwell, and the difference between them is mostly whether anything still registers.

studies.title: Those Who Were Given Knowledge
studies.meaning: The second purpose clause turns to the other group. Those given knowledge come to know that it is the truth from their Lord, and three things follow in order: knowing, then believing, then hearts settling low before it. The sequence is precise. Knowledge here does not end in a conclusion, it ends in a posture. The ayah then names God as the one who guides believers to a straight path, which puts the whole movement back on His side of the sentence.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, immediately after the ayat on revelation being confirmed and on hearts that fail the test. The same passage that named two kinds of failure now names one kind of recognition. Commentators read those given knowledge broadly, as people equipped to tell the sound from the counterfeit, and they report no specific occasion for the ayah.

keyTerms.note: Given here as something people were handed rather than something they acquired. The passive framing keeps knowing inside the same account of God's action as the guidance named at the close.
A verb from the word for level, low-lying ground. The same root named the humbled earlier in this surah, so the passage returns to its own vocabulary twenty ayat later.
A wide paved road, described as standing upright. The image is a route that does not bend, so following it asks for no navigation, only for staying on it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Medina held people trained in older scripture who could weigh a claim against what they already carried, and Arabia more widely prized whoever could tell a genuine line of poetry from an imitation. Discernment was an ordinary social skill with real stakes: knowing a true lineage, a sound coin, a reliable guide across country. This ayah sets revelation in front of that same faculty.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb describing hearts sinking low here shares its root with the word for the humbled twenty ayat earlier in the same surah, where good news was announced to them. The root comes from a term for flat, low-lying ground. The surah introduces the word as a title and then, much later, shows the state it names actually happening.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah treats knowledge as something with a bodily destination. It does not stop at assent; it travels through belief into a lowering of the heart, and no step in the sequence leaves the knower standing above what is known. That is a specific claim about learning: understanding which leaves a person elevated has stopped short. Guidance is then named as God's act rather than the learner's achievement.

crossReferences.why: Names those firm in knowledge as the ones who respond rightly to what is unclear in revelation.
Shows people given knowledge earlier falling on their faces when the recitation reaches them.
States that it is those with knowledge among God's servants who stand in awe of Him.

studies.applyIt: Think about the last thing you learned that genuinely changed how you behave, and how long the gap was between understanding it and doing anything at all. This ayah puts knowing, believing and a heart lowering into one unbroken sequence. Pick something you already know is true and close the gap on it this week, in some small way.

studies.title: In Doubt Until The Hour
studies.meaning: Doubt is described as a condition rather than a conclusion. Those who reject will not stop being uncertain about it, and the ayah names the two things that will end that state, neither of them an argument. Either the Hour arrives on them suddenly, or the punishment of a day called barren does. The word ordinarily used of a wind carrying no rain, and of a woman who bears no child, is here attached to a day. That is the ayah's strangest turn.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, closing the passage on how revelation is received. The surah has just described those given knowledge arriving at certainty. This ayah gives the opposite trajectory and refuses to present it as a decision anyone took. Commentators report no specific occasion and read the line as summarising the two receptions the surah has been setting against each other.

keyTerms.note: A word for unsettled uncertainty rather than considered denial. It describes a state someone remains inside, which is why the sentence uses a verb meaning to continue without ceasing.
An adverb of abruptness used repeatedly of the Hour. Its force is that no preparation is possible, so the arrival has no relation to whether anyone was expecting it.
Used elsewhere of a childless woman and of a wind that brings no rain. Attached to a day it means one that produces nothing after it, with no following day at all.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Barrenness was the heaviest word in that vocabulary. A childless line ended, and a wind carrying no rain meant a season without grazing and animals sold at a loss. Both were disasters with no remedy and no appeal. Attaching the word to a day would have landed instantly on listeners for whom the barren wind and the childless household were the two shapes of a future closing.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for barren appears four times in the Quran. Elsewhere it describes a wind that destroys rather than waters, and a woman's astonishment at being told she would bear a child in old age. Here alone it is attached to a day, which turns a word about lineage and rainfall into a statement about time running out.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah describes rejection as continuing uncertainty rather than as a settled position, which is a more accurate and less flattering account than either side usually gives. It also identifies what will end the uncertainty, and it is not evidence. That places a limit on argument: the passage does not promise that a better case would resolve the doubt, only that something outside the argument eventually will.

crossReferences.why: Describes the Hour arriving suddenly upon people who had denied the meeting with God.
Asks whether they await the Hour, noting that its signs have already come to them.
Uses this same word for barren of the wind sent against Aad, its other application.

studies.applyIt: Notice a question you have kept permanently open, the one you always mean to settle later. Ask honestly whether more information would actually close it, or whether staying undecided is doing something for you. This ayah describes doubt that never resolves on its own terms, and recognising the shape of it is the useful part.

studies.title: Sovereignty On That Day
studies.meaning: A single ownership is declared and everything else follows from it. Sovereignty on that day belongs to God, who judges between them, and the two outcomes are then set out as one balanced pair. Those who believed and did good are in gardens of ease; those who rejected the signs have a punishment described as humiliating. The adjective is the striking choice. Not painful, which the Quran uses far more often, but degrading, which answers something quite specific.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The surah has spent this section on people who taunted the community and demanded the promised reckoning arrive at once. These two ayat answer by describing the moment when the question of who holds authority is no longer open. Commentators read the phrasing about sovereignty as a statement about that day's clarity, not as a claim that God's rule is intermittent.

keyTerms.note: The word for actual dominion, the power a king holds over territory. Placed first in the sentence, it fronts the fact of ownership before anything is said about what is done with it.
From a root for softness and pleasant living. It describes comfort in the body as much as joy in the mind, which is why the gardens are named by this word rather than by reward.

From a verb meaning to render something contemptible. The choice names an injury to standing rather than to the body, which answers people whose objection to the message was what it cost them socially.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Standing was the currency of Arabian life. A man's worth was his lineage, his hospitality and the number of people obliged to him, and a public loss of face could ruin a family more thoroughly than a lost caravan. Much of the early opposition in Mecca came from men who could not afford to be seen following someone of lesser rank. A punishment named as humiliating meets that exactly.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase declaring sovereignty on that day occurs twice in the Quran, here and in the twenty-fifth surah, where the same day is called hard on those who rejected the message. The word chosen here for a humiliating punishment appears in eight places, while the text's far more common pairing joins punishment with pain rather than with disgrace.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The pairing of outcomes rests on a premise stated first: the authority to judge. Placing sovereignty ahead of the verdict makes the judgement an exercise of ownership rather than an intervention from outside. The two outcomes then answer human motives directly, ease for those who endured hardship and loss of face for those who guarded their standing. Neither is left abstract, and neither is described in the same register.

crossReferences.why: Carries the same declaration of sovereignty that day, calling it hard on those who rejected.
States that no soul will hold any power over another that day, the command being God's.
Asks whose the sovereignty is that day, and answers with God, the One, the Overwhelming.

studies.applyIt: Notice this week where you are actually spending effort to protect how you look: an email rewritten four times, a story adjusted for one particular listener. Just count the instances. This passage names loss of standing as a real punishment because it knows what people will pay to avoid it, and the counting teaches more than any resolution.

studies.title: Provision For Those Who Left
studies.meaning: The subject is people who emigrated for God's cause and then either were killed or simply died. The passage puts both endings in one sentence and treats them identically, which is its main work. The promise that follows is emphatic in the Arabic, and it is phrased as provision rather than as reward. The second ayah adds an entry into a place they will find pleasing, and closes with two names for God, one for knowledge and one for restraint.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, and commentators connect the passage to those who had left Mecca and Abyssinia behind. Some of the emigrants died of illness or old age rather than in fighting, and reports describe a real anxiety in the community about whether those deaths counted the same. The passage answers by naming both endings without ranking them, which is how the classical sources read it.

keyTerms.note: The verb means to leave and to sever, not merely to travel. It names a break with a place and with a kin group at once, which is what made the departure so costly.
The verb carries two emphatic markers at once in Arabic, one opening and one closing, so the promise is stated about as forcefully as the language allows a sentence to state anything.
A name describing restraint in someone with full power to act. Placed after knowledge, it says God sees everything and still holds back, which is why the two appear as a pair.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Leaving a tribe in that world meant leaving the only protection that existed. A man without kin could be robbed with nobody obliged to answer for him, and property left behind was simply absorbed by those who stayed. The emigrants to Medina arrived without land or trade, often housed by strangers. To die in that state, of a fever rather than in a battle, could look from outside like a life spent for nothing.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase naming God the best of providers occurs five times in the Quran, and its speakers vary widely, including Jesus asking for a table to be sent down from heaven. Here it closes a promise made to people who had lost every portable thing they owned, which sets the word for provision at the far end of a passage about dispossession.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage refuses a hierarchy that communities under pressure build almost automatically, in which those who die dramatically outrank those who do not. Both endings are named and given the same sentence. It also chooses the vocabulary of provision rather than of payment, which frames what follows as continued care from the same source rather than as a settling of accounts. Nothing here is described as owed.

crossReferences.why: Describes those killed in God's cause as living and provided for with their Lord.
Says the reward is secured for one who leaves home and is overtaken by death on the way.
Warns against calling those killed in God's cause dead, though the living cannot perceive it.

studies.applyIt: Think of someone you know whose hardest years produced nothing anyone could point at: a carer, a person who moved countries and never quite landed. Say something to them this week that names the cost rather than the result. This passage puts two very different endings in one sentence and declines to rank them, which is a rarer instinct than it sounds.

studies.title: Pardoning And Forgiving
studies.meaning: A response is described in careful terms. Someone answers an injury with something equal to it, and is then wronged a second time, and in that case God's help is promised emphatically. The remarkable part is the ending. Having just described a permitted response, the ayah closes on two names for God that both mean the opposite of retaliation: one for effacing an offence entirely, the other for covering it over. Permission and character are set side by side without either being withdrawn.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in the section that opened with permission for the community to defend itself. The ayah returns to that subject after the passage on emigration and provision. Commentators note that this surah keeps pairing what is allowed with what is better, and they read the two divine names at the close as pointing past the response just described rather than as cancelling it.

keyTerms.note: A word for exact equivalence. It sets the measure of a response at the size of the injury, so anything beyond that falls outside what the sentence is describing at all.
From a root meaning to exceed and to seek past a limit. The passive puts the excess entirely on the other side, describing a second injury after the accounts had been made level.
An intensive form from a root meaning to efface, as wind erases a track in sand. It describes an offence removed rather than one forgiven while still remembered.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Retaliation between tribes ran on an unwritten arithmetic and constantly overshot it. A killing was answered with two, an insult with a raid, and feuds lasted generations because nobody could agree when the sum was settled. Poets kept the score in verse that outlived the men involved. A measure setting a response at exactly the size of the injury was a real constraint there, and stopping at it was the harder half.
studies.didYouKnow: The two names closing this ayah, pardoning and forgiving, appear together in only one other place in the Quran, near the opening of a surah that begins with a woman bringing her complaint to God. Both times the pair arrives at the end of a passage about a wrong done inside a relationship rather than on a battlefield.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah does two things that pull in different directions and lets both stand. It permits a measured response and attaches God's help to it, then names God by two qualities that describe not responding at all. That refuses to collapse the tension into a rule. What it establishes is that a permitted act and the best act are not always the same, and it leaves the distance between them visible.

crossReferences.why: States the same equivalence, then names the reward of whoever pardons and sets things right.
Sets a response at the size of the injury and calls patience better for the patient.
Records equal recompense and then says remitting it counts as expiation for the one who does.

studies.applyIt: Take a grievance where you are certain you are owed something, and work out precisely what would make you level: the number, the apology, the exact sentence. Then leave it there for a week without acting on any of it. This ayah measures a response exactly and then ends on two names for letting it go, and holding both is the whole exercise.

studies.title: He Slides Night Into Day
studies.meaning: A reason is given for what came before, and it is drawn from the sky rather than from law. God slides the night into the day and the day into the night, and the verb chosen is one of insertion rather than exchange. The image is of one thing entering another gradually, which is exactly what a changing day length looks like from the ground. The ayah then closes on two names, hearing and seeing, attaching attention to power.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in a run of ayat that each open by supplying a reason for the statement before them. The surah has just described a permitted response and God's help, and here it grounds that help in something the audience could verify without argument. Commentators note that this whole section builds its case from observed nature rather than from reports.

keyTerms.note: A verb for making one thing enter into another, used of a thread going through a needle. It describes gradual encroachment rather than replacement, which is why translations reaching for merging still fall short.
The night is named first and the day second, following a reckoning in which a day begins at sunset. The order in this ayah is not arbitrary; it follows how the calendar was actually kept.
An intensive form for one whose seeing penetrates. Paired with hearing, it closes an ayah about celestial mechanics with two words that concern attention paid to people.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Everyone in that world watched the length of the day for practical reasons. Grazing, travel, the hours a caravan could move before the heat and the hours it moved after dark all shifted with the season, and the shift was gradual enough to be noticed only across weeks. Nobody had a clock. One encroaching on the other was the most familiar slow change available to observation.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb describing night entering day occurs in four places in the Quran, and in every one of them it appears twice inside the same ayah, once in each direction, never singly. Each of those four passages surrounds it with statements about God's knowledge or command, so the same observation carries the same argument wherever it appears.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah argues from continuity rather than from spectacle. Nothing dramatic is offered as proof; what is offered is the one process nobody can catch happening and nobody can doubt has happened. Placing hearing and seeing at the end links that scale to this one, so the God who moves the boundary of night is the same one attending to a single grievance. Both are held in one sentence.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the same observation almost word for word inside a closely parallel run of ayat.
Uses the identical phrase and closes on God's knowledge of what hearts contain.
Sets the same merging beside bringing the living from the dead, as one continuous act.

studies.applyIt: Watch one sunset this week from beginning to end, the whole twenty minutes, without a screen in your hand. You will not be able to name the moment it becomes night. That is this ayah's point made with your own eyes, and it costs almost nothing to check for yourself.

studies.title: The Land Turns Green
studies.meaning: Two reasons follow one another. The first is a claim about reality: God is the Real, and what is called on beside Him is the empty thing. The Arabic sets the two nouns against each other with a pronoun of emphasis in each, so it reads as a verdict rather than as a comparison. Then the argument turns physical. Water comes down and the earth becomes green, and the passage closes on two names describing what is subtle and what is fully informed.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. This section of the surah argues by pointing rather than by disputing, and commentators observe that the same sequence of claims recurs almost verbatim in a later surah. No occasion of revelation is attached to it. The audience being addressed included people who acknowledged God while also calling on other powers, which is the position the first ayah takes aim at.

keyTerms.note: The word covers truth in speech and reality in fact at once. Applied to God with the definite article it says He is what actually is, which sets up the contrast with what only appears to be.
From a root meaning to be useless or come to nothing. It does not mean false in the sense of mistaken, but hollow, a thing that will not hold weight when it is leaned on.
An intensive form describing earth taking on green rather than possessing it. The word occurs once in the Quran, and it names a change of state rather than a colour.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Rain in the Hijaz was infrequent and sudden, and the transformation after it was fast enough to feel improbable. Ground that had been stone-coloured for months carried green within days, and grazing appeared where there had been nothing to graze. Whole clan movements were planned around where it had fallen. The link between water arriving and life arriving was not a metaphor there but the year's most consequential fact.
studies.didYouKnow: These two ayat and those around them run almost word for word parallel to a sequence in the thirty-first surah, which repeats the claim about the Real and the empty, the same divine names for self-sufficiency and praise, and the description of night entering day. Two long passages in different surahs tracking each other this closely is unusual in the Quran.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage sets a claim about reality beside an agricultural observation and treats the two as one argument. What is real is what produces; what is empty produces nothing. The greening earth is offered not as a wonder but as evidence of a working cause, and the closing names, one for what operates unseen and one for what is fully informed, describe a God at work in small processes rather than only in large ones.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the claim about the Real and the empty in almost identical wording.
Points at earth revived after its death as the pattern for reviving the dead.
Uses the stirring of earth after rain as direct evidence that the dead will be raised.

studies.applyIt: Find something growing near you that you did not plant: moss on a wall, a weed in a crack, a tree older than your street. Look at it for a full minute knowing that nothing you do is holding it there. This passage argues from exactly that observation, and it works better outdoors than it does on a page.

studies.title: Rich Beyond Any Need
studies.meaning: Two clauses, and the second explains the first. Everything in the heavens and on the earth belongs to God, and the reason ownership on that scale changes nothing about Him is given in two names. He is free of need, and He is praised. The first is the more unusual: it describes not abundance but the absence of any lack, which means what He owns is not a supply He draws on. Praise is then joined to it in the same breath.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in the run of short ayat that ground the surah's argument in what God is rather than in what has happened. Commentators note that this exact sentence appears again in a later surah, inside the same sequence of claims, and they read the pairing of the two names as the point: wealth without need, and praise that does not depend on anything being received.

keyTerms.note: The ordinary Arabic word for rich, but applied to God it works by negation. What it asserts is the absence of any lack rather than the size of a holding.
A form meaning both praised in fact and deserving of praise. Placed directly after self-sufficiency, it rules out any idea of a God who needs the praise being offered.
The sentence opens with the possessive rather than with the thing possessed, which in Arabic fronts the claim. Ownership is stated before anything owned has been named.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Wealth in Arabia was visible and precarious: camels, dates, a stake in a caravan. A rich man was rich in front of people, and his standing depended on spending in front of them too, since generosity had to be witnessed to count for anything. Praise was part of that economy, bought and sold through poets. A name joining wealth to praise would call the whole arrangement to mind, then deny its logic.
studies.didYouKnow: This sentence about everything in the heavens and the earth belonging to God, closing with the two names for self-sufficiency and praise, appears again almost identically in the thirty-first surah, inside a sequence that parallels this one for several ayat together. The pairing of those two names occurs in five places across the Quran.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The two names correct each other. Saying God owns everything might suggest accumulation; saying He is free of need removes that, and saying He is praised keeps the self-sufficiency from reading as indifference. What emerges is ownership without appetite. That has a direct consequence for worship, since nothing offered supplies anything, which is the conclusion this surah already reached about flesh and blood.

crossReferences.why: Carries the same sentence and the same two names, inside a closely parallel sequence.
Turns the pair around, naming people as the ones in need and God as free of it.
Reaches the same conclusion by another route, denying that anything offered reaches God.

studies.applyIt: Notice the next time you give something and feel a small expectation form: of thanks, of being remembered, of it counting. Do not suppress it, just watch it appear. This ayah pairs owning everything with needing nothing, and the distance between that and how giving usually works in us is worth looking at squarely, once.

studies.title: He Holds Up The Sky
studies.meaning: Three things are set in a row and the listener is asked to look at each. What is on the earth has been made serviceable, ships run on the sea by His command, and the sky is held back from falling. The third is the strange one, because it names a disaster that has not happened and offers it as evidence. The ayah asks you to count an absence as an act, then closes with two names for gentleness and mercy toward people.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, continuing the passage that argues from what can be observed. The surrounding ayat each open with a form of the question do you not see, and commentators treat the sequence as one argument built from ordinary sights. No occasion of revelation is reported. The mention of ships carried weight in Medina, whose trade connected outward to Red Sea routes.

keyTerms.note: A verb for putting something to work under another's use. It implies neither ownership nor a permission granted to the user, only that the thing has been arranged to serve.
A verb of gripping and holding back. Applied to the sky it makes stability an active hold rather than a settled condition, so nothing stays up by simply being up.
A name for tenderness of a close and particular kind, usually paired with mercy. It arrives at the end of an ayah about cosmic restraint, which is where its force comes from.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Ships were the least controllable technology of the age. A vessel on the Red Sea depended on wind, season and reefs, and losses were routine enough that voyages were financed in shares to spread the risk. Land travel was different, since a caravan could stop and wait. At sea there was no stopping, and everyone knew families who had put money on a hull that never came back.
studies.didYouKnow: The clause about the sky being held back from falling on the earth occurs in this exact form only once in the Quran. The ayah names three things and only the third is a negative, an event prevented rather than an event caused, which is an unusual thing to offer as evidence of anything at all.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage treats continuation as an act rather than as a default. That is a specific claim: the world is not running on its own momentum with God occasionally intervening, it is being held. The exception clause matters too, since permission for the sky to fall is reserved rather than denied. And the ayah ends by naming tenderness, so the hold being described is characterised as care and not merely as force.

crossReferences.why: States that God holds the heavens and earth lest they cease, and no one else could.
Names the sky and the earth standing firm by His command as one of His signs.
Describes the sea made serviceable and ships ploughing through it, seeking His bounty.

studies.applyIt: Pick one thing that has simply not gone wrong lately: your back, the boiler, a friendship that could easily have frayed. Name it once today as something being held rather than as something fine. This ayah asks you to count an absence as an event, and that is a habit of attention more than it is a belief.

studies.title: He Gave You Life
studies.meaning: A three-stage sequence is given without elaboration: He gave you life, He will cause you to die, He will bring you to life again. Then a flat verdict about the human being, that he covers over what he was given. The second ayah changes subject and tone. Every community has been given its own devotions, which they themselves perform, so the argument over whose forms are correct is set aside. The instruction that follows is to call people, not to contend with them.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The community was living among others with long-established practice, and the pilgrimage passage earlier in the surah had described forms of worship in detail. Commentators read the second ayah as closing off one particular kind of argument, over ritual rather than over God, and they note that it tells the messenger not to be drawn in rather than telling him how to win.

keyTerms.note: An intensive form from the root meaning to cover over. Ingratitude in Arabic is burying a benefit rather than failing to feel one, which is why the same root also carries denial.
A participle built from the same word as the rite named immediately before it. The doubling ties the practice to the community that keeps it, and this form occurs once in the Quran.

keyTerms.gloss: let them not wrangle with you
keyTerms.note: From a root for pulling something away, as two people tug at a single object. The image is a contest over possession, which is what an argument about rites usually turns out to be.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Ritual was identity in that world. What a group ate, when it fasted, which direction it faced and what it said over an animal marked out who its people were, and disputes over these details ran hot precisely because they were the visible boundary between communities. Arguing about a form was never only about the form. It was a claim about who belonged with whom.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for performing a rite in the second ayah is built from the very same root as the word for the rite itself, used in the same breath, and that participle occurs only once in the Quran. The construction ties a practice tightly to the people who keep it, so the sentence resists any reading in which their rite is borrowed.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Setting the three stages of life beside a rebuke for ingratitude locates the human failure precisely. It is not disbelief in the sequence but a refusal to register that any of it was given. The second ayah then draws a boundary around dispute: the shared ground is God, and forms are conceded to those who keep them. Calling is separated from contending, and only one of the two is instructed.

crossReferences.why: Sets out the same sequence of life, death and return, and asks how they can disbelieve.
States that each community was given a law and a way, leaving the difference standing.
Sets the terms for argument with earlier scriptural communities, in the best manner.

studies.applyIt: Think of the last disagreement you had about how something religious should be done, rather than about whether it is true. Ask what would actually have been lost by letting it go. This passage separates inviting from wrangling and instructs only the first, which is a distinction most arguments never get anywhere near.

studies.title: God Will Judge Between You
studies.meaning: Two short ayat handle the case where the argument continues anyway. The instruction is not to answer the point but to hand it over: God knows best what you are doing. Then the second ayah names when the matter will be settled, and the phrasing is careful. God will judge between you, plural on both sides, concerning what you used to differ about. Nobody is told who will win. The disagreement is not resolved, it is moved to a competent authority.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, following directly on the instruction not to be drawn into dispute over forms of worship. The community was living among groups with older scripture and long-settled practice, and the surah has just conceded that each keeps its own devotions. Commentators read these two ayat as supplying the response for the case where that concession is not accepted.

keyTerms.note: From a root for twisting strands into a rope. An argument in this sense is something wound tighter with every turn, which is exactly the dynamic the instruction is meant to interrupt.
A comparative form, so the sentence says God knows more than the speaker does about what the other side is doing. That framing removes the speaker's standing to judge, not only his obligation.
From a root meaning to come after or take another's place. Difference here is people walking separate ways rather than holding opposed propositions, which describes communities rather than debates.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabia had no courts in any settled sense. Disputes went to an arbitrator both sides agreed to accept, often a man from a neutral clan with a reputation for fairness, and the whole system depended on finding someone neither party could dismiss. Handing a matter to an agreed judge and stopping the argument there was a recognised move, and everyone understood exactly what it meant.
studies.didYouKnow: The reply given here contains no counter-argument at all. It is four words in Arabic, and it shifts the subject from the content of the dispute to the knowledge of the one being disputed about. The Quran uses this pattern repeatedly, closing an exchange by naming God's knowledge rather than by scoring the point.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage puts a limit on what argument is for. It does not claim the disagreement is unimportant, since the second ayah promises a judgement on exactly that content. What it denies is that the judgement is available now, or to either party. That reframes disputes between communities as unfinished rather than as won, and it takes from the believer the role of settling them.

crossReferences.why: States that God will judge between disputing communities on the matters they differ over.
Puts the same handover into a prayer, asking God to judge between His servants.
Instructs the messenger to say God will gather them, with no argument between the sides.

studies.applyIt: The next time an argument reaches its third round, notice that you already know it will not end. Try saying only that you see it differently, and stop there. This passage gives a reply with no counter-argument inside it, and using one feels like losing for roughly a day, and then it stops feeling that way.

studies.title: That Is In A Book
studies.meaning: A question that expects agreement, then a claim, then a second claim easy to read past. God knows what is in the heaven and the earth. That knowledge is in a book. And that is easy for God. The third statement does the unusual work. It anticipates an objection nobody has voiced, that recording everything would be an enormous labour, and dismisses the question of scale as irrelevant before anyone can raise it.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, closing the sequence about disputes being deferred to judgement. Having said that God will judge what people differ over, the surah states how a record for such a judgement exists. Commentators read the book here as the comprehensive register of what is and what will be, and they do not attach a specific occasion to the ayah.

keyTerms.note: Indefinite here, which keeps the sentence from specifying which record is meant. The word covers both the act of writing and the thing written, so it names registration more than an object.
From a root meaning small in amount or easily flowing. The word treats a limitless record as a light matter, which is this ayah's way of denying that effort applies to God at all.
A question shaped to secure agreement rather than to seek information. It addresses a single listener, narrowing a cosmic statement to something one person is being asked to concede.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Writing existed in Arabia but was costly and uncommon. Records were kept by trained memory, and a written document was reserved for what really mattered: a treaty, a debt, a marriage settlement. Anyone hearing that something was in a book understood the claim as permanence rather than as storage. What was written could be produced later, in front of witnesses, once memories had drifted apart.
studies.didYouKnow: The ayah stacks three statements introduced by the same emphatic particle, one after another, so the sentence gains weight with each repetition rather than developing an argument. The middle statement is four words long in Arabic and says only that this is in a book, and that short clause is the entire ground for the judgement promised just before it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah joins knowledge to record, which is a stronger claim than knowledge alone. A God who knows might still be imagined forgetting; a God whose knowledge is written cannot be. That is what makes the deferred judgement of the previous ayah credible rather than merely promised. The final clause then removes effort from the picture entirely, so nothing about the arrangement is described as costly.

crossReferences.why: Extends the same written record down to a falling leaf and a seed in the dark.
States that nothing escapes your Lord, and that all of it stands in a clear record.
Says every affliction was already in a book before it was brought into being.

studies.applyIt: Write down one thing today that you would otherwise trust yourself to remember: what someone actually said, or what you actually promised. Notice a week later how differently a written line behaves from a remembered one. This ayah rests a promise of judgement on exactly that difference, and the experiment is cheap.

studies.title: No Warrant Was Sent Down
studies.meaning: The objection made here is unusual, because it is not that the other powers are weak. It is that nothing authorises them. Two lacks are named in sequence: God sent down no warrant for them, and those calling on them have no knowledge about them either. The practice therefore rests neither on revelation nor on investigation. The ayah closes with a flat statement that wrongdoers have no helper, which answers the practical hope such worship was built on.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The surah has been arguing with people whose religion was inherited rather than argued for, and this ayah puts the question of grounds directly. Commentators note that the Quran repeatedly frames worship of other powers as a claim requiring evidence rather than as a matter of preference. No specific occasion is reported for the ayah.

keyTerms.note: The word later used as the ordinary title for a ruler. In the Quran it carries the sense of proof that confers authority, so the demand here is for credentials rather than for force.
Indefinite and negated, so the sentence denies any knowledge at all rather than sufficient knowledge. The two lacks together close both routes, one from revelation and one from investigation.
From the root for coming to someone's aid at need. It names the exact function these other powers were called on for, and the ayah's last word denies it to those calling.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Religion in Arabia was largely a matter of inheritance. A clan kept the shrine it had always kept and honoured the powers its fathers honoured, and asking why was not a normal question to put. The demand for a warrant introduced a category most listeners had never applied to worship at all, and the reply recorded again and again was simply that this is what our fathers did.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for warrant used here is the same one that later became the ordinary Arabic title for a ruler. In the Quran it carries the sense of an authorising proof, so the ayah is asking for credentials rather than for power, and the demand is made of a practice rather than of any person holding it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah treats worship as a claim that carries a burden of proof. That is a considerable move: it grants that a practice may be sincere and still be unfounded, and it refuses to let inheritance count as grounds. It also names the two ways a thing could be known, from what God sends down and from what people can find out, and closes both, leaving nothing behind the practice except habit.

crossReferences.why: Records the reply that they follow what they found their fathers doing, without knowledge.
States that certain names were invented, with no warrant sent down for any of them.
Says most of them follow only conjecture, which avails nothing at all against truth.

studies.applyIt: Pick one practice in your own life you would call religious and ask, without defensiveness, where you first learned it. Some things will have a source behind them and some will only have a habit. This ayah is not attacking habit. It is asking you to know which is which, and that takes an afternoon at most.

studies.title: Recognised On Their Faces
studies.meaning: The reaction is described physically before it is named. Clear signs are recited, and the refusal can be read in the faces of those rejecting; they come close to laying hands on the reciters. Then the response, which is not a rebuke but an offer of information: shall I tell you of something worse than that. The answer given is the Fire, and the sentence turns their fury into a comparison of two evils, of which their present anger is the smaller.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in the surah's closing argument. The scene described, recitation met with visible fury and near violence, was familiar from the Meccan years and continued in encounters afterwards. Commentators do not attach a single occasion to the ayah and read it as describing a recurring situation rather than one particular incident.

keyTerms.note: The word means what is rejected or disowned, from the verb meaning not to recognise. Read in a face, it names an expression that disowns what it has just heard before any word is spoken.
A verb for laying hands on someone with force. It occurs once in the Quran, and the sentence says they nearly do it, which holds the description at the edge of violence.
A noun for where something ends up after becoming what it becomes. It names an outcome arrived at rather than a place travelled to, which is why it closes so many warnings.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Public recitation was a performance in a culture that took performance seriously. Poetry was recited at markets and fairs, judged aloud on the spot, and a devastating verse could damage a clan's standing for years. Audiences reacted openly, with praise or with fury, and reciting something unwelcome in a public space was a genuinely risky act. The near-violence here describes an ordinary setting turning.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb describing the move to seize someone occurs only once in the Quran, and the sentence keeps it as something they nearly do rather than something they do. The word for the refusal read on their faces is the same term used elsewhere in this very surah for the wrong that a community turns people away from.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage answers rage with proportion rather than with force. It concedes that the anger is real and then places it on a scale, which is a way of declining to meet it on its own terms. It also treats a facial expression as legible evidence, assuming that rejection shows itself before it is ever argued. What is offered in reply is information, not defence.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same word for the wrong a community turns people away from, in a different sense.
Shows mockery aimed at the messenger himself the moment they see him, in the same register.
Records opponents urging each other to drown out the recitation with noise of their own.

studies.applyIt: Notice this week the moment your face changes before you have decided anything: reading a message, hearing a name. It happens a beat ahead of thought. This ayah reads refusal off faces because faces are honest, and catching your own doing it once is more informative than any amount of reflection afterwards.

studies.title: They Cannot Create A Fly
studies.meaning: The ayah announces a parable and asks for attention before giving it, which is rare. Then the illustration: those called on beside God could not create a fly if they all combined for the purpose, and if the fly took something from them they could not get it back.
